To upholster means to cover a piece of furniture — typically a seat like a chair, sofa, or bench — with soft padding and a protective outer material (such as fabric or leather), making it both comfortable to sit on and attractive to look at.

Picture a bare wooden chair. It's hard, stiff, and uncomfortable after a few minutes. When you upholster it, you transform it into something cushioned and finished. You attach soft filling underneath (like foam or cotton), and then wrap it neatly in an outer covering — fabric, leather, velvet, and so on. That full process, from stuffing to finished covering, is what "upholster" describes.

Three things work together in upholstering:

  1. A support layer underneath (like woven webbing or coil springs, to hold the shape)
  2. Padding or filling (foam, cotton wadding, or similar soft material)
  3. An outer covering (fabric, leather, vinyl, suede, etc.)

All three are part of the job. Without padding, the furniture stays hard. Without the outer covering, the padding frays apart. The word "upholster" refers to the whole act of putting all of this together.

The word is used for anything meant to be sat on, leaned against, or rested on comfortably:

  • Armchairs, dining chairs, office chairs
  • Sofas and couches
  • Ottomans and footstools
  • Benches (window seats, piano benches)
  • Car seats, bus seats, train seats
  • Headboards (the padded backboard of a bed)

If a surface is meant for human contact and comfort, it can be upholstered.

One of the most frequent situations where this word appears is re-upholstering: stripping away the old, worn-out covering and padding from a piece of furniture, and replacing it with fresh materials.

Say your old sofa has faded, torn fabric and flattened foam. Instead of buying a new sofa, you take it to an upholstery shop and have it re-upholstered — fresh foam, new fabric of your choice, and it looks (and feels) brand new again. Re-upholstering is very popular because it saves money, extends the life of furniture, and lets you change the colour or texture to suit a new style.

Upholstering always accomplishes two goals at the same time: comfort (through padding and filling) and presentation (through the outer covering). Both are inseparable from the word's meaning. A chair with only foam but no fabric is not upholstered. A chair with only fabric but nothing soft underneath is also not upholstered. The word implies the complete treatment — structure, softness, and a neatly finished surface.

Also, pay attention to this: when describing what something is covered in, you'll often see the preposition "in" used — not "with." So people say "upholstered in leather" or "upholstered in red velvet." Both "in" and "with" are used, but "in" is more natural and more common.

The skilled craftsperson who upholsters furniture is called an upholsterer. It is a trade that requires knowledge of different materials, tools (like staple guns, needles, and tack strips), and furniture construction. Upholstery shops take in furniture and either upholster new pieces or restore old ones.

• Upholstery (noun): Has two closely related meanings.
    • The craft or trade itself: "He trained in upholstery for two years."
    • The materials (the padding and covering) on a piece of furniture: "The car's upholstery was soft black leather."
  • Upholstered (adjective): Describes furniture that has been given this treatment. "She bought an upholstered bench for the bedroom."
  • Upholsterer (noun): The person who performs this work professionally.

• "The carpenter made the frame, and the upholsterer upholstered it in a deep burgundy velvet."
  • "She decided to upholster the dining chairs herself using a staple gun and some linen fabric."
  • "The car manufacturer upholstered the premium seats in full-grain leather."
  • "It took him three days to upholster the sofa, but it looked completely new when he was done."
  • "Rather than throwing out her grandmother's old armchair, she had it re-upholstered in a soft sage-green fabric."
  • "The old wooden bench in the hallway was upholstered with thick foam and covered in a striped cotton."

To upholster = to fit furniture (especially seating) with padding and an outer covering (fabric, leather, etc.) to make it soft, comfortable, and visually finished. It is both a craft and a process, done by a skilled upholsterer, and applies to chairs, sofas, car seats, benches, headboards, and more. When done to restore old furniture, it is called re-upholstering.
